themes.label: Profanity / taboo insults used in political disagreement
defining_features: profanity_or_taboo_language present (e.g., explicit profanity, sexual taboo terms, “shit/bastards/idiot/asshole” style insults)
ridicule_or_mockery often paired with explicit insult language
high_punctuation_intensity frequently co-occurs (exclamation/caps with profanity)
themes.interpretation: Posts that rely heavily on profanity and demeaning invective toward people or groups are more likely to be moderated negatively (remove), even when discussing politics/policy.

themes.label: Calls to action / direct directives (vote, protest, leave, perform legal/punitive actions)
defining_features: call_to_action present (imperatives such as “vote tomorrow!”, “THROW THE BUMS OUT!!!”, “Don’t like it here then leave.”)
second_person_direct_address or direct audience prompts (e.g., rhetorical questions or “Would YOU…?”) tied to an instruction
policy_prescription_present sometimes appears as an action-oriented directive
themes.interpretation: Action-oriented language is common across both labels. Removal appears more frequent when directives escalate toward punitive/forceful targeting or accompany abusive language.

themes.label: Gun policy / self-defense / firearm regulation debate
defining_features: primary_policy_domain includes guns/firearms (e.g., concealed carry, gun reform, Second Amendment, gun violence policy)
policy_prescription_present with specific reform measures (waiting periods, bans, registry, background checks, red-flag laws)
often includes causal_claim_present linking gun laws to deaths/shootings
themes.interpretation: Gun-policy content is prominent and often kept when it includes policy prescriptions or structured critique, but moderation may remove when paired with extreme slurs/abuse or violent/punitive directives.

themes.label: Causal and evidentiary claims about harm, corruption, or hypocrisy
defining_features: causal_claim_present (cause-effect or correlational chains, e.g., “looser gun laws… correlate with higher deaths”)
factual_assertion_vs_speculation (strong event reporting with concrete figures) OR conspiratorial_framing about grifting/corruption
economic_cost_benefit_framing present in some remove examples (comparative harm/cost statements)
themes.interpretation: Moderation signals suggest that strong causal/evidence style arguments alone don’t determine removal; removals align more with extreme claims when combined with dehumanization, profanity, or punitive language.

themes.label: Second-person direct address and rhetorical engagement
defining_features: second_person_direct_address (using “you/your” to instruct or accuse)
rhetorical_question present (e.g., “Would YOU…?” “Well regulated? NAH!”)
call_to_action sometimes realized as direct prompts to the audience
themes.interpretation: Directly addressing the reader/target is common in both groups; removal is more likely when the address is hostile or coupled with taboo/profane escalation.

themes.label: Us-vs-them / polarized blame framing
defining_features: us_vs_them_framing (group-level hypocrisy, polarization, or blame attribution)
target_directionality with party/group targets (Democrats/Republicans/left/right; mirror retargeting often reflects this)
sometimes paired with moral condemnation language (normative_moral_language)
themes.interpretation: Polarized group framing appears evenly in both labels; moderation likely depends more on accompanying hostility (profanity/dehumanization/punitive directives) than on polarization alone.

themes.label: Named entities, organizations, accounts, and policy/program references
defining_features: named_proper_nouns_density (political figures, organizations like NRA, Medicaid, SNAP, IRA, named laws)
hashtag_or_mention_pattern and quote_or_attribution_embedding often appear alongside named references
topic specificity via proper nouns (e.g., program acronyms, legislation titles)
themes.interpretation: Reference density is mostly compatible with keep outcomes; it becomes more problematic when combined with abusive/prohibitive rhetoric.

themes.label: Quotation/attribution embedding of slogans or cited statements
defining_features: quote_or_attribution_embedding present (quoted speech with attributed speaker or quoted policy slogans)
quote_or_attribution_embedding correlates with high_punctuation_intensity (quotation marks)
quote_or_attribution_embedding sometimes used to counter a slogan
themes.interpretation: Embedding quotes/slogans occurs across both outcomes; moderation effect appears indirect—quotes themselves aren’t the determinant.

themes.label: Conditional/contrastive argumentative structures
defining_features: conditional_if_then_structure (If… then…, either/or, “if we stop looking…”)
contrastive_but_however_structure (but/however to rebut or set hypocrisy contrasts)
anaphora_or_parallelism (structured contrast like “In a world where… But unfortunately…”)
themes.interpretation: Well-structured conditional/contrast rhetoric is common and often compatible with keep labels; removal is more linked to toxicity layers (profanity, dehumanization, punitive directives).

themes.label: High punctuation intensity / emphasis (exclamation marks, all caps, many quotes)
defining_features: high_punctuation_intensity (heavy !, caps, intense quotation emphasis)
all_caps_emphasis appears in some remove cases
often accompanies imperatives and profanity
themes.interpretation: Strong emphasis (caps/exclamation/profanity adjacency) correlates with removals more often, likely reflecting heightened confrontational tone.

cross_cutting_themes: Gun policy content (appears within multiple themes: policy prescriptions, causal claims, and conditional/prescriptive directives)
High-toxic rhetoric layers: profanity/taboo insults + high punctuation/emphasis frequently co-occur and connect to remove outcomes across different topic domains (guns, abortion, parties, candidates)
Direct engagement style: second-person addressing and rhetorical questions/calls to action span both keep and remove themes, but become more risky when paired with insult language
Polarization and blame structures: us-vs-them framing and named-entity references combine with causal/evidentiary claims to form targeted political accusations
